title: Going to your brother (Matthew 18:15–17)
hook: Jesus' steps for a wrong between people: speak privately first, aiming to win the person back

segments.voice: Yesterday, what forgiveness isn't: not excusing, not forgetting, not staying in danger. Your line was forgive and stay safe.

Someone close does something that stings. A comment in front of others. A promise quietly dropped. There are two easy moves. One is to tell everyone else: a friend, a sibling, a group chat, anyone except the person who did it. The other is to say nothing and let it sour slowly. Jesus offers a third move, and it may be the hardest of the three, because it goes straight to the one person you'd rather avoid. Yesterday's line still stands: this is for ordinary hurts between people who are safe with each other.

In Matthew 18, Jesus lays out steps, and the order matters. Step one, in the King James Bible: "if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." Alone. Before anyone else hears about it. And the goal: gained thy brother. Not won the argument; won back the person. Step two, only if step one fails: take one or two others along, "that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." That phrase comes from the Torah's own rule for fair judgment, in Deuteronomy. The witnesses aren't there to gang up. They're there to keep things fair and clear. Step three: "tell it unto the church." And if he won't hear even the church, Jesus says, "let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." Here readers part ways. Some churches read this as a step of formal discipline: the person is treated as outside the fellowship until they turn back. Other readers notice who is telling the story. The Gospel itself calls its namesake Matthew the publican, a tax collector, and Jesus ate with tax collectors. So they hear it as: start over with them, the way Jesus started with Matthew. Either way, the shape is the same. The circle begins at its smallest. The hope is that it never has to widen. Going privately protects the other person's dignity, and it gives the friendship a real chance.

Bring to mind one hurt from someone you're close to that you've told others about, or swallowed, and picture going to them alone. Find your first sentence, plain and short, what happened and how it landed on you, with no list of old grievances, and say it silently a few times until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can ask for a soft voice and a fair ear.
Going to your brother. Jesus' first step when someone wrongs you: tell them alone, hoping to win them back.
Your line: go privately first. The circle begins at its smallest. That's day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians use Matthew 18:15–17 as a guide for conflict in families, friendships and congregations; some churches build it into their rules for church discipline, and pastors coach members to go to the person privately before involving anyone else.

fork.setup: a close friend embarrassed you in front of others, and it still stings. by Jesus' steps in Matthew 18, what comes first?
options: tell a few trusted people what happened.
go to the friend alone and tell them.
bring two witnesses and confront them.
fork.reveal: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone." witnesses come only if that fails, and the church only after that.

original.note: Greek: you have gained, from a verb for making a profit; "thou hast gained thy brother" (Matthew 18:15).

trapdoor: what you thought: when someone wrongs you, call them out.
what it means: go to them alone first, to win them back; widen the circle only if that fails, and only step by step.
what a scholar hears: "two or three witnesses" echoes Deuteronomy 19:15, and the same Gospel calls its namesake "Matthew the publican" (Matthew 10:3), the very word in step three.
guess: telling someone their wrong privately, to win them back
asking a family member to settle a quarrel for you
reporting a wrong to church leaders straight away

chat.says: A coworker embarrassed me in a meeting. Should I tell the whole team what she did?
options: Jesus' first step is to go to her alone, hoping to win her back, not win the argument.
Jesus' first step is to bring two witnesses, so it's clear from the start who was wrong.
Jesus' first step is to tell it to the church, so the whole group can weigh in on it.
chat.meaning: In Matthew 18 the order matters: go alone first. The goal is gained thy brother, winning back the person; the circle widens only if that fails.

Deuteronomy.meaning: a book of the Torah, with a rule for fair judgment

heathen.meaning: an old word for someone outside the faith

publican.meaning: a tax collector, in the King James Bible

notes: Two readings of 'as an heathen man and a publican' given without ranking: formal church discipline (treated as outside the fellowship), and 'start over with them as Jesus did with tax collectors'. Confirm both are fairly described.
The hook limits the steps to ordinary hurts between people who are safe with each other, following day 1228; confirm, given that some abuse situations make private confrontation unsafe.
Greek ἐκέρδησας (aorist of κερδαίνω, to gain/profit); confirm form and gloss.
Matthew 18:15 KJV: some manuscripts lack 'against thee'; the KJV text includes it. Not mentioned in the script.
'Matthew the publican' (Matthew 10:3) is quoted as the Gospel's own wording; the script does not claim Matthew wrote the Gospel.
